nuggets.summary: Before starting Bizible, Bird had spent years executing a careful plan to save roughly $500k before ever attempting to start a company — but the 2008 financial crisis wiped out his savings and real-estate equity, leaving him $20k in debt to his own parents. The experience taught him that in startups a "perfect plan" is largely irrelevant because unpredictable external shocks can undo years of preparation; his conclusion was that founders should stop waiting for ideal financial conditions and just start, raising smaller amounts (even from friends and family) to get moving rather than trying to fully de-risk the leap first.
nuggets.quote: lesson one was plans are irrelevant in startups. Like, your perfect plan sucks. It's not going to work. Don't do it. Like, just jump, right?

nuggets.summary: Bizible's founder ran validation to an extreme: before writing any code for the pivoted product, he got three paying customers to sign checks. His broader philosophy is that lean-startup MVP thinking doesn't go far enough — the only real proof a product/market/price combination works is a customer literally paying before the product exists. He argues this is actually kinder to the customer, not a disservice, because it forces the founder to build only what people actually want rather than guessing and building the wrong thing. Even after Bizible had hundreds of customers, they kept the practice of selling roadmap items ("we don't have this yet, we'll have it by this date") before building them.
nuggets.quote: So we had this philosophy of, the only way you know that someone will buy it, that they'll buy it at a price point that you can cost-effectively build it and acquire them for, and that you're selling to the right buyer... The first version of Visible, we got three checks before we started writing code.

nuggets.summary: A concrete tactic for validating demand before building anything: run an ad (Facebook/Google) or landing page describing the product as if it already exists, and let people click through to a signup page asking for a credit card. You never actually charge the card since nothing has been built, but if people are willing to enter payment details, that's effectively proof of a sale — you can then email them saying delivery is a few weeks out. This is a cheap, direct way to test true purchase intent instead of relying on survey answers or pageviews, and it prevents months of building in the wrong direction.
nuggets.quote: if you have something that can be sold completely online, then you can run ads, you can have a website that says it's going to do what it's going to do, and then you can say, you know, sign up here and put in your credit card... Obviously, you're not going to bill it because you don't have anything done yet, but just see, will they put in their credit card? Like, essentially, you've sold it now, right?

nuggets.summary: When a startup desperately needs a role filled and the only candidates available are "good but not great," the tempting move is to hire them anyway on the logic that a mediocre person is better than an empty seat for the next six months. Bird calls this a repeated early mistake: it's true for the next six months, but the cost of eventually having to replace that person — for both the company and the person — is far higher than the short-term pain of leaving the seat open. His fix is to hold a high hiring bar even when it means letting organizational pain continue.
nuggets.quote: it's really easy to say, you know what, in the next six months we'll be better off if I have someone good in this role than if I have no one in this role... And that's true for the next six months. The problem is after that... the cost of having to replace someone, both for you and them, is way too high.

nuggets.summary: Rather than hiring specialists early (e.g., the "perfect" content marketing person), Bird prioritized hiring generalist "athletes" who could be handed any problem and run with it, plus strong culture/values fit — because in the first year you genuinely don't know what role someone will need to fill two months from now. A specialist hired for one narrow function resents or fails at being asked to do something outside that lane (e.g., a content marketer told to work a trade-show booth), whereas a generalist adapts. He pairs this with prioritizing perseverance and long-haul commitment over resume strength for the first ~10 hires, since early employees may face missed payroll and pay cuts.
nuggets.quote: hiring for culture and then hiring for that... generalist kind of athlete role. Because you don't know two months from now what you're going to be doing or what you need them doing. And specializing too early, you go get like the perfect content marketing person because you need content marketing. Well, and then you tell them like, I need you to go to a field event and work a booth, right? And they're like, I've never done that before.

nuggets.summary: One of Bizible's earliest customer-acquisition wins came from exploiting a narrow, time-boxed opportunity: Salesforce announced it was deprecating a free integration ("Salesforce for Google AdWords") that required a script tag on customers' websites. Bird's team crawled the web looking for that script tag, harvested the resulting list of domains, scraped phone numbers off those sites, and cold-called each one with an urgent message that their integration was dying in two months and Bizible had the replacement. That single hack-driven campaign landed roughly 40 customers in six weeks — a result that wouldn't have been possible through generic outbound or paid ads, illustrating that under-exploited, narrow, expiring opportunities can outperform conventional channels disproportionately.
nuggets.quote: we crawled the web. So it had a script tag. You had to put a script tag on your website for this thing to work... We crawled the domains to get a phone number, and then that was our lead list... And we signed up, like, 40 customers in six weeks or something like that.

nuggets.summary: Instead of cold-pitching investors at random, Bird targeted VCs who already had a pre-existing "thesis" matching the startup's category — for example, Madrona's Len Jordan had a standing thesis around "accountable media" (ad-spend accountability), which lined up with Bizible's ROI-measurement pitch, and Scale's Stacey Bishop had a thesis around marketing ROI specifically. Every round Bizible raised came from investors who, before ever talking to Bird, already believed in the space. The takeaway: use public info (e.g., Crunchbase) to find VCs with a stated thesis in your exact category rather than pitching broadly, since walking in already-aligned massively increases odds versus knocking on random doors.
nuggets.quote: these guys had thesis around what we're doing. So I think if you can find, you know, if you're doing a mobile app for gaming or whatever, it's like go find VCs that have been investing in that space because they'll have a thesis around, you know, mobile gaming... it's way better than just, like, knocking on random doors, right?

nuggets.summary: Bird argues founders systematically underweight how much capital they'll actually need, and that worrying about dilution is close to irrelevant compared to the risk of running out of cash. His own experience: he went out to raise $700,000 for the Madrona round and ended up raising $1.7 million — and needed every dollar of it, despite having built a plan around the smaller number. His broader claim is that he's never met a founder who regretted raising too much and retaining less equity, but has met many who regretted running out of money; the advice is to raise as much as you can get, on whatever terms, because equity dilution is a much smaller problem than insolvency.
nuggets.quote: I went out asking for $700,000 and we raised $1.7 million. And we needed every dime of it, you know, in the end... I've never met an entrepreneur that was like, that their regret was like, oh, I had this exit. But, you know, I had 10% of the company. If I would have had 12, it would have been a lot better.

nuggets.summary: To raise an angel round of a specific target size, Bizible used "soft circling" — getting informal, conditional commitments from angels ("if you get to $300k raised, I'll write a check") before any money changed hands — and stacked roughly $400,000 of these soft commitments. They then used that pool as leverage on both sides simultaneously: telling VCs the round was nearly full so they'd need to move fast to get an allocation, and telling angels that VC interest meant the round could close without them if they didn't commit now. The mechanism deliberately manufactures urgency and scarcity in a negotiation where investors otherwise have every incentive to simply wait.
nuggets.quote: we started to get like commitments from angels. Like, you know, if you get to $300,000, I'll write a check, right?... So kind of using the two to create urgency... investors are, you know, they have no incentive to write a check... So you need to find a way to, to create scarcity or urgency.

nuggets.summary: A related fundraising tactic exploited the social calendars of angel investors: Bizible mapped out which angels regularly met with each other (e.g., a recurring Tuesday brunch among a cluster of ten investors) and then deliberately emailed several of them the traction update the night before that meeting, so the topic would organically surface in their group conversation the next morning. The goal was to manufacture a sense of independent, converging interest ("buzz") among a connected group of investors rather than pitching each one in isolation.
nuggets.quote: we would target a group... then what we would do is to try to figure out when do those 10 people meet with each other... Monday night, send them both an email about all your traction, right? So that when they meet on Tuesday morning, maybe they'll... bring it up.

nuggets.summary: Bizible burned roughly two years believing they had solved sales scaling when they only had proof it worked for the first two reps. Their first two salespeople (co-founders Alex and Andy) performed extremely well, so they assumed the same hiring profile would replicate — but the third, fourth, and fifth hires all failed, revealing that early individual sales success (often driven by founder-level product knowledge and credibility) doesn't automatically transfer to a repeatable hiring/training system. The eventual fix was promoting their top rep into a training/management role, against the board's explicit advice, and later bringing in a dedicated VP of Sales — but only after roughly two years of unproductive reps.
nuggets.quote: The second salespeople, Alex and Andy, um, were crushing it... and then it was like the third one failed, the fourth one failed, the fifth one failed... we burned two years, uh, of just not, of having two sales reps that were productive.

nuggets.summary: Bird pushes back on the common founder assumption that they can hire salespeople out of the gate to handle sales while they focus elsewhere. His claim is that no hired salesperson — however good — can sell as well as a founder early on, because customers respond to the cachet and authority of talking to the CEO/co-founder, and only a founder can credibly promise future roadmap items or speak with total product authority. The implication: founders should expect to personally be the primary salesperson for a meaningful stretch before they can effectively hand off or scale the function.
nuggets.quote: one mistake that entrepreneurs make is they think that they're gonna hire salespeople out of the gate. It's like, no, no, you're the salesperson. You're the guy. You gotta go sell... no one's going to sell like a co-founder does.

nuggets.summary: Bird advises against ever preparing a formal "Plan B" while trying to make a startup work, arguing that simply having a fallback option makes it more likely you'll actually use it — pulling energy and belief away from the primary path at the exact moments of maximum difficulty. He frames startup success as requiring "irrational perseverance" and explicitly says the expected value of starting a company is worse than staying at a stable, high-paying job (citing friends at Microsoft), so committing "for the money" or "as a trial" doesn't work — you have to be all-in irrationally, without a rational hedge.
nuggets.quote: if you're thinking about a plan B, then don't do it. Uh, it's just cause it, cause you will use plan B... you can't do it for the money. You can't do it like as a trial. Um, you, you, you've gotta just be kind of all in irrationally.

nuggets.summary: Bird identifies a specific, common failure mode among founders: because entrepreneurs are natural builders, their instinct is to rush past the problem-discovery phase and get straight to building a solution once they think they've found the right problem. He says this cost his own team over a year of wasted work, and that the actual highest-leverage use of early time is not building — it's rigorously validating that the problem you've identified is the right one before you start solving it.
nuggets.quote: I see every startup do it where entrepreneurs are builders, right? And so their instinct is they don't want to spend time finding a problem. They want to spend time solving a problem... spend all your time early on finding the right problem and make sure it's the right one.

nuggets.summary: Bizible deliberately targeted the B2B segment of marketing attribution rather than competing broadly against Google/Adometry, based on an insight from Bird's time at Bing: B2B advertising makes up only a "single digit" percentage of Google's and Bing's total ad revenue. Because that segment is too small to ever become a strategic priority for a company the size of Google, Bird could be confident Google would never build dedicated B2B attribution well enough to compete — letting a small startup safely own and defend a niche that a giant is structurally incentivized to ignore, rather than one it might casually crush.
nuggets.quote: if you look at Google and Bing, you know, the percentage of media buys, like the percentage of their revenue from advertising that comes from B2B is small. It's, it's in the single digits. So I know that Google's never going to go build B2B attribution the way that they really have to because it's, it's never going to make the priority list.

nuggets.summary: Bird describes a Seattle-specific hiring asymmetry that shaped Bizible's team-building strategy: for technical talent, Seattle is unusually favorable because Microsoft and Amazon create a huge pool of engineers who actively want to leave big companies for startups, and (unlike San Francisco) there are relatively few local startups competing for them. But for B2B sales and marketing talent, Seattle is worse than San Francisco, which has a deep bench of experienced enterprise-martech sales reps. Bizible's workaround was to stop trying to hire experienced enterprise salespeople off the street and instead hire earlier-career people and build/train them internally — accepting a slower, homegrown pipeline for the function the local market couldn't supply.
nuggets.quote: for us, sales and marketing is harder to hire in San Francisco... there's not that many startups that sell the Martech and the enterprise... so you have to like, you know, you have to do more around kind of getting people and building them... you're not going to be able to hit all your hiring goals by hiring experienced people off the street.

nuggets.summary: To hire early employees despite being unable to match big-company salaries, Bird used a specific framing: pay meaningfully under market (e.g., offering $90k against a $175k Microsoft salary) but pair it with equity and an explicit "give us a year, it's an experiment for you" pitch that reduces the perceived risk of leaving a stable job. The pitch also promises salary increases once specific milestones (financing or a customer win) hit. This works because Seattle has engineers at Microsoft/Amazon with financial cushions who want startup experience, making the under-market/equity/experiment framing a viable substitute for market-rate pay.
nuggets.quote: you have to pay under market, uh, back to that, you've got to find somebody that believes in the dream... you say, look, hey, give us a year, right?... you're gonna, sure you could make, uh, you know, 175 at Microsoft. I'm going to pay you 90... in a year, once we get financing or we get this customer, I'm going to raise your salary.

nuggets.summary: Bird cites Amazon's competitive discipline as a model for avoiding complacency after finding initial success in a market: Amazon systematically "burns the boats" roughly every six months after entering a new market by cutting margins to the point that would-be competitors can't follow. The broader point is that many startups make the mistake of finding early product-market fit and then coasting, assuming the market will keep growing for them, when defensible advantage instead requires continuously re-commoditizing what you built yesterday to make room for the next differentiator.
nuggets.quote: I think Amazon is amazing at that. Um, they just, you know, they just burn the boats like every six months, right? It's like, uh, as soon as they go to a market, they just cut all the margins out. It's like, how could you follow them?
